paragraphs.text:
自然界中具有铁磁性的材料种类不算多，但它们有重要的实际用途。
在温度低于材料的居里温度、线圈电流和绕组几何保持相同的比较中，插入适当的铁芯或钢芯，可以使线圈内部的磁场增强很多倍。
增强来自材料被磁化后的贡献，不是因为线圈电流增大；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 增强的倍数也取决于材料、形状和磁化状态。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
铁磁质在适当的磁化条件下能沿外加磁场的方向被磁化，它的相对磁导率 $\mu$ 可以远远大于 1.
经过磁化后，有些铁磁性样品在撤去外加磁化场时仍保留净磁化，这叫剩磁。
剩磁不是线圈里仍有电流的证据，也不表示未经磁化的每块材料都天然是一块永久磁铁。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
铁磁质的磁导率不是固定不变的材料常数。
在温度和样品形状保持相同的实验中，它仍取决于当前磁场的强弱，以及样品此前经历过怎样的磁化过程。
因此，仅知道当前外加磁场，往往还不足以确定材料的磁化状态；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 不能给铁指定一个适用于所有情况的固定增强倍数。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
把某种铁磁质加热到它特有的居里温度以上，它会失去铁磁性的自发磁化，而不是失去对一切磁场的响应。
居里温度以法国学者居里的名字命名；
把磁化的铁针充分加热到这一温度以上，它原来因剩磁而明显吸引铁物体的能力就会消失。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
原教材列出的温度值是：铁 $753^\circ\mathrm{C}$，镍 $365^\circ\mathrm{C}$，钴 $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$；
一些铁磁性合金的居里温度小于 $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$。
这些数值仅作为原教材的历史记载保留，其中一些与目前通行的参考值并不一致；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
不能把它们作为当前材料的可靠居里温度，或仅仅视为精度较低的现代测量值。
具体材料的转变温度需要依据其成分和测量资料确定。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
为了描述材料的磁性状态，本教材引入一个称为**磁化强度**的量。
考虑放在足够长螺线管中的长而均匀的铁棒，并在中央区域采用近似均匀、同向且可忽略端部退磁影响的模型；
在指定的非零外加场和磁化历史下，把内部磁感应强度写成 $B=\mu B_0$。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
其中 $B$ 是有材料时的内部总磁感应强度，$B_0$ 是相同线圈电流在没有材料时产生的磁感应强度；
两者之差表示材料的磁化贡献。
本教材用 $I$ 表示这个差值，所以它具有磁感应强度的单位，不是电流，也不是现代通常以安培每米为单位的磁化强度；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
两种磁化量需要通过真空磁导率换算。
这里的相对磁导率只表示给定状态下的比值，不是对所有场强和历史都成立的常数。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif
"Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 代入(13-1)式，在上述模型和指定的非零外加场状态下，也可以写成：

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif
"Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
$I$ 与 $B_0$ 的关系比较复杂，因为铁磁质的 $\mu$ 本身也与 $B_0$ 有关，还取决于磁化历史。
在温度、样品形状和磁化过程已经指定时，$I$ 随 $B_0$ 变化的曲线叫做**磁化曲线**。
这种曲线可以通过实验求得，测量思路参见 §133；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 指定过程不同，不能假定所得曲线完全相同。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
从已经退磁、净磁化近似为零的铁样品出发，在温度保持不变且低于居里温度、磁场缓慢增大的实验中，磁化强度 $I$ 起初随 $B_0$ 的增大近似按直线增加，如图 301 所示。
随后样品接近饱和：尽管 $B_0$ 继续增大，材料的磁化贡献已近似保持不变，但这不表示内部总磁场停止增大。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
原教材用微小环形电流取向来解释这一点：饱和时，它们产生的磁矩已经近似沿场取向，所以 $B_0$ 再增大也不能明显增加这一部分的场。
这是一种定性的磁矩模型，不是把电子自旋当成小球的机械转动；
从磁畴的角度看，材料内部原有的自发磁化区域逐渐改变大小和取向，使净磁化增加，最终接近同向饱和。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
每种铁磁性材料都有自己的磁化特性，不能拿一种材料的磁化曲线代替所有材料。
比较曲线时，还要说明温度、样品形状以及磁化前的状态和施加磁场的过程。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
实际的 $I$ 与 $B_0$ 关系比图 301 的初始曲线更复杂：相同的当前磁场，可能对应不同的磁化状态。
磁化不仅取决于此时的场，也取决于先前是否磁化过、达到过多强的场以及场怎样增减；
图 301 只表示从退磁状态开始增场的过程。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
在相同温度、样品几何和缓慢变场条件下，从饱和状态减小磁化场时，磁化强度 $I$ 并不沿原来的增场曲线返回，通常会保留较大的磁化。
这种对磁化历史的依赖叫做**磁滞**；
磁畴壁移动和磁矩转向可能受到阻碍，因此撤去外加场后不一定恢复原来的状态。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
$I$ 与 $B_0$ 的一个完整磁化过程如图 302 所示；
这里保持温度和样品形状不变，忽略背景场，并缓慢改变外加磁化场。
从退磁状态出发，沿 $oa$ 增场，过程类似于图 301 的初始磁化曲线，在 $a$ 点达到近似饱和。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
再把 $B_0$ 减小到 0，磁化沿 $ab$ 段减小；
当 $B_0=0$ 时，磁化强度仍不为零，图中的 $I=ob$ 表示**剩磁**。
撤去外加磁化场后，样品仍能产生自身的磁场，表现为永久磁铁；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
这来自材料保留的磁化，不是线圈继续通电，也不是说此时样品内部总磁场为零。
此时不能把磁导率当作有限恒量，直接用它乘以零来否定剩磁。
接着在反方向增大外加磁感应强度 $B_0$，磁化逐渐减小，直到原教材所记的 $B_{0k}=oc$ 时，净磁化才为零；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
这里图上的距离表示反向场的大小，不是把反向场说成正方向。
原教材把 $B_{0k}$ 称为**矫顽力**，用来表示使当前样品的净磁化降到零所需的反向磁化场尺度；
它不是机械力，也不是样品内部总磁感应强度，现代常用的磁场强度单位需另作换算。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
继续反向增场，到 $a'$ 点达到反向饱和，再减场到零并向原方向增场，最后回到 $a$ 点。
在温度固定、材料没有偏置且正反磁化过程相称的理想模型中，这条闭合曲线关于 $o$ 点对称，称为**磁滞回线**。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
原教材把俄国物理学家 A. G. 斯托列托夫（1839～1896）介绍为最早仔细研究铁磁性材料磁化特性的学者。
A. G. 斯托列托夫采用了这样的磁化方法：在闭合铁环上绕导线，再让导线通电，使铁环磁化。
闭合磁路有助于减小开放铁棒端部的退磁影响；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 材料的磁化由线圈产生的磁化场建立，不能把材料中的磁化强度误认为导线电流。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
不同铁磁性材料的磁滞回线可以有不同形状，这是比较它们磁性的重要依据。
这种比较要在明确的温度、样品形状、磁化历史和变场条件下进行，不能把回线形状看成脱离实验条件的固定图形。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
按磁化和去磁的难易，可以把铁磁性材料分成**软磁材料**和**硬磁材料**，这里的软硬不是机械硬度。
在相同坐标尺度和可比磁化条件下，图 303a 示意软磁材料的较窄、面积较小的回线，并在本图中表现为较小的剩磁和矫顽力。
铁、某些品种的钢以及坡莫合金（铁镍合金）可以属于软磁材料；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
软磁材料容易反复改变磁化方向，但不能仅凭回线面积小，就断言所有软磁材料的剩磁都很小。
图 303b 示意硬磁材料的较宽、面积较大的回线，并在本图中表现为较大的剩磁和矫顽力。
较稳定的剩磁和较强的抗去磁能力使这类材料适合制作永久磁铁；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 比较时仍须说明温度、磁化幅度和样品条件。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
软磁材料可用作变压器、发电机和电动机等装置的铁芯。
在需要交变磁场的工作条件下，铁芯反复磁化和去磁，需要外界做功，其中一部分能量在每个磁滞循环中转变为热。
对温度和样品条件固定、变场足够缓慢的完整循环，按正确的物理坐标和单位换算后，磁滞回线所围面积表示单位体积材料每个循环的磁滞损耗；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
本教材用磁感应强度表示磁化量，因此还需考虑真空磁导率的换算，求整个铁芯的损耗则还需考虑体积。
不能把纸面上量得的面积直接当成整个铁芯的功。
在相同磁化幅度和可比条件下，较窄回线的软磁材料通常比较宽回线的硬磁材料有更小的磁滞损耗；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 实际装置还有涡流等损耗，不能只靠回线面积断言总损耗大小。

自然界中具有铁磁性的材料种类不算多，但它们有重要的实际用途。
在温度低于材料的居里温度、线圈电流和绕组几何保持相同的比较中，插入适当的铁芯或钢芯，可以使线圈内部的磁场增强很多倍。
增强来自材料被磁化后的贡献，不是因为线圈电流增大；
增强的倍数也取决于材料、形状和磁化状态。

铁磁质在适当的磁化条件下能沿外加磁场的方向被磁化，它的相对磁导率 $\mu$ 可以远远大于 1.
经过磁化后，有些铁磁性样品在撤去外加磁化场时仍保留净磁化，这叫剩磁。
剩磁不是线圈里仍有电流的证据，也不表示未经磁化的每块材料都天然是一块永久磁铁。

铁磁质的磁导率不是固定不变的材料常数。
在温度和样品形状保持相同的实验中，它仍取决于当前磁场的强弱，以及样品此前经历过怎样的磁化过程。
因此，仅知道当前外加磁场，往往还不足以确定材料的磁化状态；
不能给铁指定一个适用于所有情况的固定增强倍数。

把某种铁磁质加热到它特有的居里温度以上，它会失去铁磁性的自发磁化，而不是失去对一切磁场的响应。
居里温度以法国学者居里的名字命名；
把磁化的铁针充分加热到这一温度以上，它原来因剩磁而明显吸引铁物体的能力就会消失。

原教材列出的温度值是：铁 $753^\circ\mathrm{C}$，镍 $365^\circ\mathrm{C}$，钴 $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$；

这些数值仅作为原教材的历史记载保留，其中一些与目前通行的参考值并不一致；

不能把它们作为当前材料的可靠居里温度，或仅仅视为精度较低的现代测量值。
具体材料的转变温度需要依据其成分和测量资料确定。

自然界中具有铁磁性的材料种类不算多，但它们有重要的实际用途。
在温度低于材料的居里温度、线圈电流和绕组几何保持相同的比较中，插入适当的铁芯或钢芯，可以使线圈内部的磁场增强很多倍。
增强来自材料被磁化后的贡献，不是因为线圈电流增大；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 增强的倍数也取决于材料、形状和磁化状态。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
铁磁质在适当的磁化条件下能沿外加磁场的方向被磁化，它的相对磁导率 $\mu$ 可以远远大于 1.
经过磁化后，有些铁磁性样品在撤去外加磁化场时仍保留净磁化，这叫剩磁。
剩磁不是线圈里仍有电流的证据，也不表示未经磁化的每块材料都天然是一块永久磁铁。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
铁磁质的磁导率不是固定不变的材料常数。
在温度和样品形状保持相同的实验中，它仍取决于当前磁场的强弱，以及样品此前经历过怎样的磁化过程。
因此，仅知道当前外加磁场，往往还不足以确定材料的磁化状态；

paragraphs.text:

一些铁磁性合金的居里温度小于 $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$。

不能把它们作为当前材料的可靠居里温度，或仅仅视为精度较低的现代测量值。

paragraphs.text:

paragraphs.text:
两种磁化量需要通过真空磁导率换算。

"Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 代入(13-1)式，在上述模型和指定的非零外加场状态下，也可以写成：

"Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:

这种曲线可以通过实验求得，测量思路参见 §133；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 指定过程不同，不能假定所得曲线完全相同。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
从已经退磁、净磁化近似为零的铁样品出发，在温度保持不变且低于居里温度、磁场缓慢增大的实验中，磁化强度 $I$ 起初随 $B_0$ 的增大近似按直线增加，如图 301 所示。
随后样品接近饱和：尽管 $B_0$ 继续增大，材料的磁化贡献已近似保持不变，但这不表示内部总磁场停止增大。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
原教材用微小环形电流取向来解释这一点：饱和时，它们产生的磁矩已经近似沿场取向，所以 $B_0$ 再增大也不能明显增加这一部分的场。
这是一种定性的磁矩模型，不是把电子自旋当成小球的机械转动；
从磁畴的角度看，材料内部原有的自发磁化区域逐渐改变大小和取向，使净磁化增加，最终接近同向饱和。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
每种铁磁性材料都有自己的磁化特性，不能拿一种材料的磁化曲线代替所有材料。
比较曲线时，还要说明温度、样品形状以及磁化前的状态和施加磁场的过程。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
实际的 $I$ 与 $B_0$ 关系比图 301 的初始曲线更复杂：相同的当前磁场，可能对应不同的磁化状态。
磁化不仅取决于此时的场，也取决于先前是否磁化过、达到过多强的场以及场怎样增减；
图 301 只表示从退磁状态开始增场的过程。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
在相同温度、样品几何和缓慢变场条件下，从饱和状态减小磁化场时，磁化强度 $I$ 并不沿原来的增场曲线返回，通常会保留较大的磁化。
这种对磁化历史的依赖叫做**磁滞**；
磁畴壁移动和磁矩转向可能受到阻碍，因此撤去外加场后不一定恢复原来的状态。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
$I$ 与 $B_0$ 的一个完整磁化过程如图 302 所示；
这里保持温度和样品形状不变，忽略背景场，并缓慢改变外加磁化场。
从退磁状态出发，沿 $oa$ 增场，过程类似于图 301 的初始磁化曲线，在 $a$ 点达到近似饱和。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
再把 $B_0$ 减小到 0，磁化沿 $ab$ 段减小；
当 $B_0=0$ 时，磁化强度仍不为零，图中的 $I=ob$ 表示**剩磁**。
撤去外加磁化场后，样品仍能产生自身的磁场，表现为永久磁铁；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
这来自材料保留的磁化，不是线圈继续通电，也不是说此时样品内部总磁场为零。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
这里图上的距离表示反向场的大小，不是把反向场说成正方向。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
继续反向增场，到 $a'$ 点达到反向饱和，再减场到零并向原方向增场，最后回到 $a$ 点。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
原教材把俄国物理学家 A. G. 斯托列托夫（1839～1896）介绍为最早仔细研究铁磁性材料磁化特性的学者。

paragraphs.text: 材料的磁化由线圈产生的磁化场建立，不能把材料中的磁化强度误认为导线电流。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:

这种比较要在明确的温度、样品形状、磁化历史和变场条件下进行，不能把回线形状看成脱离实验条件的固定图形。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
按磁化和去磁的难易，可以把铁磁性材料分成**软磁材料**和**硬磁材料**，这里的软硬不是机械硬度。
在相同坐标尺度和可比磁化条件下，图 303a 示意软磁材料的较窄、面积较小的回线，并在本图中表现为较小的剩磁和矫顽力。
铁、某些品种的钢以及坡莫合金（铁镍合金）可以属于软磁材料；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
软磁材料容易反复改变磁化方向，但不能仅凭回线面积小，就断言所有软磁材料的剩磁都很小。
图 303b 示意硬磁材料的较宽、面积较大的回线，并在本图中表现为较大的剩磁和矫顽力。
较稳定的剩磁和较强的抗去磁能力使这类材料适合制作永久磁铁；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 比较时仍须说明温度、磁化幅度和样品条件。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
软磁材料可用作变压器、发电机和电动机等装置的铁芯。
在需要交变磁场的工作条件下，铁芯反复磁化和去磁，需要外界做功，其中一部分能量在每个磁滞循环中转变为热。
对温度和样品条件固定、变场足够缓慢的完整循环，按正确的物理坐标和单位换算后，磁滞回线所围面积表示单位体积材料每个循环的磁滞损耗；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
本教材用磁感应强度表示磁化量，因此还需考虑真空磁导率的换算，求整个铁芯的损耗则还需考虑体积。
不能把纸面上量得的面积直接当成整个铁芯的功。
在相同磁化幅度和可比条件下，较窄回线的软磁材料通常比较宽回线的硬磁材料有更小的磁滞损耗；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: 实际装置还有涡流等损耗，不能只靠回线面积断言总损耗大小。

blocks.text: 印刷页 318

blocks.text:
自然界中具有铁磁性的材料种类不算多，但它们有重要的实际用途。
在温度低于材料的居里温度、线圈电流和绕组几何保持相同的比较中，插入适当的铁芯或钢芯，可以使线圈内部的磁场增强很多倍。
增强来自材料被磁化后的贡献，不是因为线圈电流增大；

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: 增强的倍数也取决于材料、形状和磁化状态。

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:

剩磁不是线圈里仍有电流的证据，也不表示未经磁化的每块材料都天然是一块永久磁铁。

居里温度以法国学者居里的名字命名；
把磁化的铁针充分加热到这一温度以上，它原来因剩磁而明显吸引铁物体的能力就会消失。

自然界中具有铁磁性的材料种类不算多，但它们有重要的实际用途。
在温度低于材料的居里温度、线圈电流和绕组几何保持相同的比较中，插入适当的铁芯或钢芯，可以使线圈内部的磁场增强很多倍。
增强来自材料被磁化后的贡献，不是因为线圈电流增大；
增强的倍数也取决于材料、形状和磁化状态。

铁磁质在适当的磁化条件下能沿外加磁场的方向被磁化，它的相对磁导率 $\mu$ 可以远远大于 1.
经过磁化后，有些铁磁性样品在撤去外加磁化场时仍保留净磁化，这叫剩磁。
剩磁不是线圈里仍有电流的证据，也不表示未经磁化的每块材料都天然是一块永久磁铁。

铁磁质的磁导率不是固定不变的材料常数。
在温度和样品形状保持相同的实验中，它仍取决于当前磁场的强弱，以及样品此前经历过怎样的磁化过程。
因此，仅知道当前外加磁场，往往还不足以确定材料的磁化状态；
不能给铁指定一个适用于所有情况的固定增强倍数。

把某种铁磁质加热到它特有的居里温度以上，它会失去铁磁性的自发磁化，而不是失去对一切磁场的响应。
居里温度以法国学者居里的名字命名；
把磁化的铁针充分加热到这一温度以上，它原来因剩磁而明显吸引铁物体的能力就会消失。

原教材列出的温度值是：铁 $753^\circ\mathrm{C}$，镍 $365^\circ\mathrm{C}$，钴 $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$；
一些铁磁性合金的居里温度小于 $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$。
这些数值仅作为原教材的历史记载保留，其中一些与目前通行的参考值并不一致；

不能把它们作为当前材料的可靠居里温度，或仅仅视为精度较低的现代测量值。
具体材料的转变温度需要依据其成分和测量资料确定。

为了描述材料的磁性状态，本教材引入一个称为**磁化强度**的量。
考虑放在足够长螺线管中的长而均匀的铁棒，并在中央区域采用近似均匀、同向且可忽略端部退磁影响的模型；
在指定的非零外加场和磁化历史下，把内部磁感应强度写成 $B=\mu B_0$。

其中 $B$ 是有材料时的内部总磁感应强度，$B_0$ 是相同线圈电流在没有材料时产生的磁感应强度；
两者之差表示材料的磁化贡献。
本教材用 $I$ 表示这个差值，所以它具有磁感应强度的单位，不是电流，也不是现代通常以安培每米为单位的磁化强度；

两种磁化量需要通过真空磁导率换算。
这里的相对磁导率只表示给定状态下的比值，不是对所有场强和历史都成立的常数。

$I$ 与 $B_0$ 的关系比较复杂，因为铁磁质的 $\mu$ 本身也与 $B_0$ 有关，还取决于磁化历史。
在温度、样品形状和磁化过程已经指定时，$I$ 随 $B_0$ 变化的曲线叫做**磁化曲线**。
这种曲线可以通过实验求得，测量思路参见 §133；
指定过程不同，不能假定所得曲线完全相同。

从已经退磁、净磁化近似为零的铁样品出发，在温度保持不变且低于居里温度、磁场缓慢增大的实验中，磁化强度 $I$ 起初随 $B_0$ 的增大近似按直线增加，如图 301 所示。

paragraphs.text: Relatively few kinds of material in nature are ferromagnetic, but they have important practical uses.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: At a temperature below the material's Curie temperature, inserting a suitable iron or steel core can strengthen the field inside a coil many times over while its current and winding geometry remain the same.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
The extra field comes from the magnetized material, not from an increase in coil current;
the enhancement also depends on the material, its shape, and its magnetic state.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Under suitable magnetizing conditions, a ferromagnetic material can become magnetized along the applied field, and its relative permeability $\mu$ can be much greater than 1.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
After magnetization, some ferromagnetic specimens retain a net magnetization when the applied magnetizing field is removed;
this is remanence.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Remanence is not evidence that current is still flowing in the coil, nor does it mean that every unmagnetized piece is already a permanent magnet.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The permeability of a ferromagnetic material is not a fixed material constant.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Even at the same temperature and with the same specimen shape, it depends on the present field strength and on the specimen's previous magnetizing history.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
Knowing only the present applied field is therefore often insufficient to determine the magnetic state;
iron cannot be assigned a single enhancement factor valid in every situation.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Heating a ferromagnetic material above its particular Curie temperature removes its ferromagnetic spontaneous magnetization, not every possible response to a magnetic field.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The temperature is named after the French scientist Curie (居里);

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: an iron needle heated sufficiently above this temperature loses the conspicuous ability to attract iron that came from its remanent magnetization.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The original textbook lists iron at $753^\circ\mathrm{C}$, nickel at $365^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and cobalt at $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: some ferromagnetic alloys have Curie temperatures below $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: These numbers are retained only as the original textbook's historical report. Some do not agree with reference values in current use;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: they must not be treated as reliable Curie temperatures for present-day materials, or merely as less precise modern measurements.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: A particular material's transition temperature must be established from its composition and measurement data.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: To describe the material's magnetic state, this textbook introduces a quantity called **magnetization**.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Consider a long, uniform iron rod inside a sufficiently long solenoid, using a model in which the central fields are approximately uniform and aligned and end-related demagnetizing effects are negligible;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: at a specified nonzero applied field and magnetic history, write the internal flux density as $B=\mu B_0$.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Here $B$ is the total internal magnetic flux density with the material present, while $B_0$ is the flux density produced by the same coil current without the material;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: their difference measures the material's magnetic contribution.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The textbook denotes this difference by $I$, so it has units of magnetic flux density, not electric current and not the amperes-per-metre units commonly used for modern magnetization;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: conversion between the magnetic quantities involves the permeability of free space.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The relative permeability here describes a ratio at the specified state, not a constant valid for all fields and histories.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif
"Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Substituting equation (13-1), within the model above and at the specified nonzero applied-field state, also gives:

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif
"Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The relation between $I$ and $B_0$ is complex because a ferromagnet's $\mu$ itself depends on $B_0$, as well as on magnetic history.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: For a specified temperature, specimen shape, and magnetizing procedure, the curve showing $I$ against $B_0$ is called a **magnetization curve**.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
It can be obtained experimentally using the measurement approach in §133;
different procedures need not produce the same curve.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: Start with a demagnetized iron specimen whose net magnetization is approximately zero, keep its temperature fixed below the Curie temperature, and increase the applied field slowly;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: initially, its magnetization $I$ rises approximately linearly with $B_0$, as shown in Figure 301 (the initial magnetization curve).

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The specimen then approaches saturation: although $B_0$ continues to increase, the material's magnetic contribution becomes nearly constant, but the total internal field need not stop increasing.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: The textbook explains this using the orientation of tiny loop currents: at saturation, their magnetic moments are nearly aligned with the field, so further increases in $B_0$ cannot substantially increase their contribution.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: This is a qualitative magnetic-moment model, not a picture of electron spin as a mechanically rotating ball;

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text: in domain language, existing spontaneously magnetized regions change their sizes and orientations, increasing the net magnetization until it approaches aligned saturation.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

paragraphs.text:
Each ferromagnetic material has its own magnetizing characteristics;

intendedParagraphs.text: Relatively few kinds of material in nature are ferromagnetic, but they have important practical uses.

At a temperature below the material's Curie temperature, inserting a suitable iron or steel core can strengthen the field inside a coil many times over while its current and winding geometry remain the same.

The extra field comes from the magnetized material, not from an increase in coil current;
the enhancement also depends on the material, its shape, and its magnetic state.
Under suitable magnetizing conditions, a ferromagnetic material can become magnetized along the applied field, and its relative permeability $\mu$ can be much greater than 1.

After magnetization, some ferromagnetic specimens retain a net magnetization when the applied magnetizing field is removed;
this is remanence.
Remanence is not evidence that current is still flowing in the coil, nor does it mean that every unmagnetized piece is already a permanent magnet.
The permeability of a ferromagnetic material is not a fixed material constant.
Even at the same temperature and with the same specimen shape, it depends on the present field strength and on the specimen's previous magnetizing history.

Knowing only the present applied field is therefore often insufficient to determine the magnetic state;
iron cannot be assigned a single enhancement factor valid in every situation.
Heating a ferromagnetic material above its particular Curie temperature removes its ferromagnetic spontaneous magnetization, not every possible response to a magnetic field.
The temperature is named after the French scientist Curie (居里);
an iron needle heated sufficiently above this temperature loses the conspicuous ability to attract iron that came from its remanent magnetization.
The original textbook lists iron at $753^\circ\mathrm{C}$, nickel at $365^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and cobalt at $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$;
some ferromagnetic alloys have Curie temperatures below $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
These numbers are retained only as the original textbook's historical report. Some do not agree with reference values in current use;
they must not be treated as reliable Curie temperatures for present-day materials, or merely as less precise modern measurements.
A particular material's transition temperature must be established from its composition and measurement data.
To describe the material's magnetic state, this textbook introduces a quantity called **magnetization**.

Consider a long, uniform iron rod inside a sufficiently long solenoid, using a model in which the central fields are approximately uniform and aligned and end-related demagnetizing effects are negligible;
at a specified nonzero applied field and magnetic history, write the internal flux density as $B=\mu B_0$.
Here $B$ is the total internal magnetic flux density with the material present, while $B_0$ is the flux density produced by the same coil current without the material;
their difference measures the material's magnetic contribution.
The textbook denotes this difference by $I$, so it has units of magnetic flux density, not electric current and not the amperes-per-metre units commonly used for modern magnetization;
conversion between the magnetic quantities involves the permeability of free space.
The relative permeability here describes a ratio at the specified state, not a constant valid for all fields and histories.
Substituting equation (13-1), within the model above and at the specified nonzero applied-field state, also gives:
The relation between $I$ and $B_0$ is complex because a ferromagnet's $\mu$ itself depends on $B_0$, as well as on magnetic history.
For a specified temperature, specimen shape, and magnetizing procedure, the curve showing $I$ against $B_0$ is called a **magnetization curve**.

It can be obtained experimentally using the measurement approach in §133;
different procedures need not produce the same curve.
Start with a demagnetized iron specimen whose net magnetization is approximately zero, keep its temperature fixed below the Curie temperature, and increase the applied field slowly;
initially, its magnetization $I$ rises approximately linearly with $B_0$, as shown in Figure 301 (the initial magnetization curve).
The specimen then approaches saturation: although $B_0$ continues to increase, the material's magnetic contribution becomes nearly constant, but the total internal field need not stop increasing.

The textbook explains this using the orientation of tiny loop currents: at saturation, their magnetic moments are nearly aligned with the field, so further increases in $B_0$ cannot substantially increase their contribution.
This is a qualitative magnetic-moment model, not a picture of electron spin as a mechanically rotating ball;
in domain language, existing spontaneously magnetized regions change their sizes and orientations, increasing the net magnetization until it approaches aligned saturation.

Each ferromagnetic material has its own magnetizing characteristics;
one material's curve cannot stand in for every material.
A comparison must also specify the temperature, specimen shape, initial magnetic state, and the procedure used to apply the field.
The actual relation between $I$ and $B_0$ is more complex than the initial curve in Figure 301: the same present field can correspond to different magnetic states.
Magnetization depends on whether the specimen was magnetized before, how strong the previous field was, and how it increased or decreased;
Figure 301 describes only increasing the field from a demagnetized state.
At the same temperature and specimen geometry, with a slowly changing field, reducing the magnetizing field from saturation does not make the magnetization $I$ retrace the increasing-field curve;

it usually retains a larger magnetization.
This dependence on magnetic history is **hysteresis**;
domain-wall motion and magnetic-moment reorientation can be impeded, so removing the applied field need not restore the initial state.
Figure 302 shows a full magnetizing sequence relating $I$ and $B_0$;
keep temperature and specimen shape fixed, neglect background fields, and change the applied magnetizing field slowly.
Starting from a demagnetized state, increase the field along $oa$, as on the initial magnetization curve in Figure 301, and reach approximate saturation at $a$.

Then reduce $B_0$ to 0, following $ab$;
when $B_0=0$, the magnetization is still nonzero, and $I=ob$ represents **remanence**.
With the applied magnetizing field removed, the specimen still produces its own field and behaves as a permanent magnet;
this comes from retained material magnetization, not continuing coil current, and it does not mean the total internal field is zero.
A finite, constant permeability multiplied by a zero applied field cannot be used here to rule out remanence.
Next, increase the applied magnetic flux density $B_0$ in the reverse direction until the net magnetization reaches zero at the textbook's $B_{0k}=oc$;
the plotted distance expresses the magnitude of the reverse field, not a claim that its direction is positive.
The textbook calls $B_{0k}$ the **coercive field**, expressing the reverse magnetizing-field scale needed to reduce this specimen's net magnetization to zero;
it is not a mechanical force or the total internal magnetic flux density, and conversion is needed to the field-strength units commonly used today.
Continue to reverse saturation at $a'$, reduce the field to zero, then increase it in the original direction until the curve returns to $a$.
In an ideal model with fixed temperature, no magnetic bias, and equivalent forward and reverse procedures, this closed curve is symmetric about $o$ and is called a **hysteresis loop**.
The original textbook credits the Russian physicist A. G. Stoletov (斯托列托夫, 1839-1896) as the first to study the magnetizing characteristics of ferromagnetic materials carefully.
A. G. Stoletov used a magnetizing method in which wire was wound around a closed iron ring and current was passed through the wire to magnetize the ring.
A closed magnetic path helps reduce the end-related demagnetizing effects of an open rod;
the coil's magnetizing field establishes the material's magnetization, which must not be mistaken for electric current in the wire.
Different ferromagnetic materials can have differently shaped hysteresis loops, an important basis for comparing their magnetic properties.

Such comparisons require specified temperatures, specimen shapes, magnetic histories, and field-changing conditions;
a loop is not a fixed shape independent of the experiment.
Ferromagnetic materials may be classified as **magnetically soft** or **magnetically hard** according to how easily they are magnetized and demagnetized;
this is not mechanical hardness.
With the same axis scales and comparable magnetizing conditions, Figure 303a illustrates a narrower, smaller-area soft-material loop, with smaller remanence and coercivity in this particular drawing.
Iron, certain steels, and permalloy, an iron-nickel alloy, can be magnetically soft;
these materials readily reverse their magnetization, but a small loop area alone does not establish small remanence for every soft material.
Figure 303b illustrates a wider, larger-area hard-material loop, with larger remanence and coercivity in this drawing.
Stable remanence and greater resistance to demagnetization make such materials suitable for permanent magnets;
comparisons must still specify temperature, magnetizing amplitude, and specimen conditions.
Magnetically soft materials can serve as cores in transformers, generators, and electric motors.
Under operating conditions that require alternating magnetic fields, the core is repeatedly magnetized and demagnetized, requiring external work;
some energy becomes heat during each hysteresis cycle.

For a complete, sufficiently slow cycle at fixed temperature and specimen conditions, the enclosed loop area, converted using the correct physical axes and units, represents hysteresis energy loss per unit material volume per cycle;
because this textbook expresses magnetization as a flux-density contribution, conversion involving the permeability of free space is needed, and the whole core's loss also depends on its volume.
An area measured on the page is not directly the work done on the entire core.
At the same magnetizing amplitude and under comparable conditions, a narrower-loop soft material usually has less hysteresis loss than a wider-loop hard material;
actual devices also have losses such as eddy-current loss, so loop area alone does not determine their total loss.

geometry.fontFamily: ui-monospace, Menlo, monospace

blocks.text: Relatively few kinds of material in nature are ferromagnetic, but they have important practical uses.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: At a temperature below the material's Curie temperature, inserting a suitable iron or steel core can strengthen the field inside a coil many times over while its current and winding geometry remain the same.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
The extra field comes from the magnetized material, not from an increase in coil current;
the enhancement also depends on the material, its shape, and its magnetic state.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: Under suitable magnetizing conditions, a ferromagnetic material can become magnetized along the applied field, and its relative permeability $\mu$ can be much greater than 1.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
After magnetization, some ferromagnetic specimens retain a net magnetization when the applied magnetizing field is removed;
this is remanence.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: Remanence is not evidence that current is still flowing in the coil, nor does it mean that every unmagnetized piece is already a permanent magnet.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: The permeability of a ferromagnetic material is not a fixed material constant.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text: Even at the same temperature and with the same specimen shape, it depends on the present field strength and on the specimen's previous magnetizing history.

geometry.fontFamily: "Songti SC", "Source Han Serif SC", "Noto Serif CJK SC", SimSun, serif

blocks.text:
Knowing only the present applied field is therefore often insufficient to determine the magnetic state;
iron cannot be assigned a single enhancement factor valid in every situation.

blocks.text: Heating a ferromagnetic material above its particular Curie temperature removes its ferromagnetic spontaneous magnetization, not every possible response to a magnetic field.

intendedParagraphs.text: Relatively few kinds of material in nature are ferromagnetic, but they have important practical uses.

At a temperature below the material's Curie temperature, inserting a suitable iron or steel core can strengthen the field inside a coil many times over while its current and winding geometry remain the same.

The extra field comes from the magnetized material, not from an increase in coil current;
the enhancement also depends on the material, its shape, and its magnetic state.
Under suitable magnetizing conditions, a ferromagnetic material can become magnetized along the applied field, and its relative permeability $\mu$ can be much greater than 1.

After magnetization, some ferromagnetic specimens retain a net magnetization when the applied magnetizing field is removed;
this is remanence.
Remanence is not evidence that current is still flowing in the coil, nor does it mean that every unmagnetized piece is already a permanent magnet.
The permeability of a ferromagnetic material is not a fixed material constant.
Even at the same temperature and with the same specimen shape, it depends on the present field strength and on the specimen's previous magnetizing history.

Knowing only the present applied field is therefore often insufficient to determine the magnetic state;
iron cannot be assigned a single enhancement factor valid in every situation.
Heating a ferromagnetic material above its particular Curie temperature removes its ferromagnetic spontaneous magnetization, not every possible response to a magnetic field.
The temperature is named after the French scientist Curie (居里);
an iron needle heated sufficiently above this temperature loses the conspicuous ability to attract iron that came from its remanent magnetization.
The original textbook lists iron at $753^\circ\mathrm{C}$, nickel at $365^\circ\mathrm{C}$, and cobalt at $1000^\circ\mathrm{C}$;
some ferromagnetic alloys have Curie temperatures below $100^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
These numbers are retained only as the original textbook's historical report. Some do not agree with reference values in current use;
they must not be treated as reliable Curie temperatures for present-day materials, or merely as less precise modern measurements.
A particular material's transition temperature must be established from its composition and measurement data.
To describe the material's magnetic state, this textbook introduces a quantity called **magnetization**.

Consider a long, uniform iron rod inside a sufficiently long solenoid, using a model in which the central fields are approximately uniform and aligned and end-related demagnetizing effects are negligible;
at a specified nonzero applied field and magnetic history, write the internal flux density as $B=\mu B_0$.
Here $B$ is the total internal magnetic flux density with the material present, while $B_0$ is the flux density produced by the same coil current without the material;
their difference measures the material's magnetic contribution.
The textbook denotes this difference by $I$, so it has units of magnetic flux density, not electric current and not the amperes-per-metre units commonly used for modern magnetization;
conversion between the magnetic quantities involves the permeability of free space.
The relative permeability here describes a ratio at the specified state, not a constant valid for all fields and histories.
Substituting equation (13-1), within the model above and at the specified nonzero applied-field state, also gives:
The relation between $I$ and $B_0$ is complex because a ferromagnet's $\mu$ itself depends on $B_0$, as well as on magnetic history.
For a specified temperature, specimen shape, and magnetizing procedure, the curve showing $I$ against $B_0$ is called a **magnetization curve**.

It can be obtained experimentally using the measurement approach in §133;
different procedures need not produce the same curve.
Start with a demagnetized iron specimen whose net magnetization is approximately zero, keep its temperature fixed below the Curie temperature, and increase the applied field slowly;
initially, its magnetization $I$ rises approximately linearly with $B_0$, as shown in Figure 301 (the initial magnetization curve).
The specimen then approaches saturation: although $B_0$ continues to increase, the material's magnetic contribution becomes nearly constant, but the total internal field need not stop increasing.

The textbook explains this using the orientation of tiny loop currents: at saturation, their magnetic moments are nearly aligned with the field, so further increases in $B_0$ cannot substantially increase their contribution.
This is a qualitative magnetic-moment model, not a picture of electron spin as a mechanically rotating ball;
in domain language, existing spontaneously magnetized regions change their sizes and orientations, increasing the net magnetization until it approaches aligned saturation.

Each ferromagnetic material has its own magnetizing characteristics;
one material's curve cannot stand in for every material.
A comparison must also specify the temperature, specimen shape, initial magnetic state, and the procedure used to apply the field.
The actual relation between $I$ and $B_0$ is more complex than the initial curve in Figure 301: the same present field can correspond to different magnetic states.
Magnetization depends on whether the specimen was magnetized before, how strong the previous field was, and how it increased or decreased;
Figure 301 describes only increasing the field from a demagnetized state.
At the same temperature and specimen geometry, with a slowly changing field, reducing the magnetizing field from saturation does not make the magnetization $I$ retrace the increasing-field curve;

it usually retains a larger magnetization.
This dependence on magnetic history is **hysteresis**;
domain-wall motion and magnetic-moment reorientation can be impeded, so removing the applied field need not restore the initial state.
Figure 302 shows a full magnetizing sequence relating $I$ and $B_0$;
keep temperature and specimen shape fixed, neglect background fields, and change the applied magnetizing field slowly.
Starting from a demagnetized state, increase the field along $oa$, as on the initial magnetization curve in Figure 301, and reach approximate saturation at $a$.

Then reduce $B_0$ to 0, following $ab$;
when $B_0=0$, the magnetization is still nonzero, and $I=ob$ represents **remanence**.
With the applied magnetizing field removed, the specimen still produces its own field and behaves as a permanent magnet;
this comes from retained material magnetization, not continuing coil current, and it does not mean the total internal field is zero.
A finite, constant permeability multiplied by a zero applied field cannot be used here to rule out remanence.
Next, increase the applied magnetic flux density $B_0$ in the reverse direction until the net magnetization reaches zero at the textbook's $B_{0k}=oc$;
the plotted distance expresses the magnitude of the reverse field, not a claim that its direction is positive.
The textbook calls $B_{0k}$ the **coercive field**, expressing the reverse magnetizing-field scale needed to reduce this specimen's net magnetization to zero;
it is not a mechanical force or the total internal magnetic flux density, and conversion is needed to the field-strength units commonly used today.
Continue to reverse saturation at $a'$, reduce the field to zero, then increase it in the original direction until the curve returns to $a$.
In an ideal model with fixed temperature, no magnetic bias, and equivalent forward and reverse procedures, this closed curve is symmetric about $o$ and is called a **hysteresis loop**.
The original textbook credits the Russian physicist A. G. Stoletov (斯托列托夫, 1839-1896) as the first to study the magnetizing characteristics of ferromagnetic materials carefully.
A. G. Stoletov used a magnetizing method in which wire was wound around a closed iron ring and current was passed through the wire to magnetize the ring.
A closed magnetic path helps reduce the end-related demagnetizing effects of an open rod;
the coil's magnetizing field establishes the material's magnetization, which must not be mistaken for electric current in the wire.
Different ferromagnetic materials can have differently shaped hysteresis loops, an important basis for comparing their magnetic properties.

Such comparisons require specified temperatures, specimen shapes, magnetic histories, and field-changing conditions;
a loop is not a fixed shape independent of the experiment.
Ferromagnetic materials may be classified as **magnetically soft** or **magnetically hard** according to how easily they are magnetized and demagnetized;
this is not mechanical hardness.
With the same axis scales and comparable magnetizing conditions, Figure 303a illustrates a narrower, smaller-area soft-material loop, with smaller remanence and coercivity in this particular drawing.
Iron, certain steels, and permalloy, an iron-nickel alloy, can be magnetically soft;
these materials readily reverse their magnetization, but a small loop area alone does not establish small remanence for every soft material.
Figure 303b illustrates a wider, larger-area hard-material loop, with larger remanence and coercivity in this drawing.
Stable remanence and greater resistance to demagnetization make such materials suitable for permanent magnets;
comparisons must still specify temperature, magnetizing amplitude, and specimen conditions.
Magnetically soft materials can serve as cores in transformers, generators, and electric motors.
Under operating conditions that require alternating magnetic fields, the core is repeatedly magnetized and demagnetized, requiring external work;
some energy becomes heat during each hysteresis cycle.

For a complete, sufficiently slow cycle at fixed temperature and specimen conditions, the enclosed loop area, converted using the correct physical axes and units, represents hysteresis energy loss per unit material volume per cycle;
because this textbook expresses magnetization as a flux-density contribution, conversion involving the permeability of free space is needed, and the whole core's loss also depends on its volume.
An area measured on the page is not directly the work done on the entire core.
At the same magnetizing amplitude and under comparable conditions, a narrower-loop soft material usually has less hysteresis loss than a wider-loop hard material;
actual devices also have losses such as eddy-current loss, so loop area alone does not determine their total loss.
